Policy4OOD: A Knowledge-Guided World Model for Policy
Intervention Simulation against the Opioid Overdose Crisis
Yijun Ma*, Zehong Wang*, Weixiang Sun, Zheyuan Zhang, Kaiwen Shi, Nitesh Chawla, Yanfang Ye†

Our code and data have been released in
https://github.com/antman9914/Policy4OOD.

This enables policymakers

implementation. Second,counterfactual reasoning: the frame-
work should assess what would have happened had alternative
policies been enacted. This capability supports retrospective evalu-
ation of policy decisions and identification of missed opportunities.
Third,policy optimization: given a pool of available policy in-
struments, the framework should identify the combination most
likely to minimize adverse outcomes.

The
dataset spans January 2019 to December 2024 at monthly resolution.
Dataset schema is illustrated in Figure 2.
For graph construction, each node𝑣𝑖∈𝑉 represents one of the
48 contiguous U.S. states (Alaska and Hawaii are excluded due to
geographical isolation).

All data are sourced from
authoritative public databases, including the Centers for Disease
Control and Prevention (CDC), Federal Reserve Economic Data
(FRED), StatsAmerica, and the FBI Crime Data Explorer, ensur-
ing data reliability and traceability. These descriptors are selected
based on their established relevance in opioid policy literature and
availability from authoritative national sources.
Edges𝐸 encode geographical adjacency: two states are connected
if they share a terrestrial border (point-contact excluded). This
structure captures cross-border spillover effects—including illicit
drug supply networks, population mobility, and treatment access
patterns—that have been shown to influence regional opioid dy-
namics [13]. The resulting graph contains |𝐸|= 194edges.

To capture these, we refer
to graph learning methods [28, 29, 46, 57, 73] and represent each
state by encoding its local spatial context. For state𝑠, we extract its
𝐾-hop neighborhood subgraphG(𝐾)𝑠 containing all states reachable
within𝐾 hops along geographical adjacency edges. We encode this
context through recursive neighborhood aggregation [22, 30, 55].

For state 𝑠 at time𝑡, we
collect all concurrently enacted policy documents and jointly ex-
tract structured triplets using a large language model. Constructing
a single KG from co-deployed policies—rather than separate KGs
per document—naturally captures cross-policy interactions: shared
entities link provisions from different policies, revealing how multi-
ple interventions jointly shape the regulatory landscape.

The first branch uses the state
embeddingh(𝑡)𝑠 to retrieve strategies relevant to the current socioe-
conomic context; the second uses the mean-pooled KG embedding
¯e(𝑠,𝑡) = 1|VKG| ˝𝑗 e𝑗 to retrieve strategies aligned with the enacted
policies.

Each
node corresponds to a partial policy sequence, and the world model
serves as a fast simulator: at each tree level, the selected policy is
injected into the historical window, the model produces a trajectory,
and the window is advanced. The search follows standard MCTS
phases—selection via UCT [31], expansion, rollout simulation, and
backpropagation—and after𝐵 simulations, the optimal sequence is
extracted by following the most-visited children at each level.

Evaluation Settings.For all the methods, we use data during 2019-
2022 for training, and predict overdose deaths during 2022-2023
and 2023-2024 during validation and testing respectively. Input and
output window size are set as𝑇ℎ = 6and 𝑇𝑓 = 6. We adopt Mean
Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) [1, 2]
for evaluation. Except for the overall MAE and RMSE, we further
report prediction errors over different forecasting horizons, includ-
ing the first three future months (MAE1−3,RMSE1−3) and the last
three future months (MAE4−6,RMSE4−6), to assess short-term and
longer-term forecasting performance respectively. We consider two
settings for forecasting task evaluation: (1) Standard forecasting,
where models are trained to predict future trends of opioid over-
dose deaths based on all the available historical observations. (2)
Cross-state generalization, where models are trained on data from a
randomly selected subset of 40 states and evaluated on the remain-
ing 9 unseen states. Each model is trained on 3 distinct random
seeds to reduce the influence of randomness.

GPT-4o-miniandall-MiniLM-L6-v2
are adopted for policy knowledge graph extraction and textual
feature embedding respectively. The default hyperparameters are:
hidden dimension 𝑑ℎ = 64, projected policy dimension 𝑑𝑝 = 6,
number of Transformer layers𝐿= 1, number of attention heads
𝑛head = 4, feed-forward dimension4 𝑑ℎ = 256, dropout rate0 .1
, EMA momentum coefficient 𝛼= 0.99, learning rate5 × 10−4
with the Adam optimizer, and early stopping patience of 10 epochs.
Simulation budget for MCTS is set as 𝐵= 1000. We conduct 3
independent runs with different random seeds and report the mean
value of all metrics.

evidence_fragments.content:
In this study, we use the trained
Policy4OOD to predict how opioid epidemic will evolve in Ten-
nessee under following three settings: (1) Advancing: advance the
implementation time of the reformation policy by six month; (2)
Replacement: replace the reformation policy with recovery housing
policy (KY H 248), meanwhile keep the implementation timeline
unchanged; (3) Removal: remove policy TN H 215 in Tennessee.
The input window is set from Jan. 2021 to Jun. 2021, and we aim to
predict the opioid epidemic evolution from Jul. 2021 to Dec. 2021.

can
not replace causally identified treatment effects. Policy4OOD does
not control for detailed confounding factors or enforce parallel
trends assumptions, and the background socioeconomic dynamics
remain fixed. Therefore, the analysis should not be interpreted as
rigorous causal inference. Besides, counterfactual outcomes are
inherently unobservable, meaning the trajectories shown for Ad-
vancing, Replacement, and Removal scenarios cannot be directly
validated against ground truth. Instead, the model’s credibility in
qualitative counterfactual reasoning rests on its factual forecasting
accuracy.

To
construct the candidate policy pool, we categorize available policies
into five domains—recovery service regulation, health insurance
coverage, funding allocation, governance oversight, and clinical
practice—and select a representative policy from each. Detailed pol-
icy descriptions are provided in Table 5(a). We conduct case studies
on Tennessee and Virginia, two states that have also consistently
experienced severe opioid overdose burdens. For each state, we aug-
ment the base policy pool with its own enacted policy documents to
form a state-specific candidate set.

As shown in Figure 5, Pol-
icy4OOD successfully recovers the policy that was actually enacted
in Tennessee during the subsequent months. For Virginia, although
the optimized policy set does not coincide with the policies that
were actually implemented, the resulting predicted trajectory yields
lower cumulative overdose deaths, suggesting that Policy4OOD
can identify potentially more effective policy combinations beyond
those historically adopted.

Future work includes expand-
ing the dataset in temporal coverage and granularity, extending
beyond overdose mortality to broader opioid-related outcomes, and
validating the counterfactual and policy optimization modules with
domain experts.

legacy_cells.B: Policy4OOD: A Knowledge-Guided World Model for Policy Intervention Simulation against the Opioid Overdose Crisis
legacy_cells.C: Yijun Ma*, Zehong Wang*, Weixiang Sun, Zheyuan Zhang, Kaiwen Shi, Nitesh Chawla, Yanfang Ye†
legacy_cells.O: Opioid overdose crisis / opioid overdose mortality
legacy_cells.S: How state-level opioid overdose mortality forecasts change under enacted or alternative policies, and which candidate policy sequence minimizes predicted cumulative overdose deaths.
legacy_cells.T: State-level records for 48 contiguous U.S. states (Alaska and Hawaii excluded); monthly data from January 2019 to December 2024.
legacy_cells.V: Compare policy interventions and select policy combinations/timing intended to reduce predicted opioid overdose deaths.
legacy_cells.AI: Monthly state-level opioid overdose mortality and socioeconomic time series (economic, demographic, and crime descriptors); policy documents represented as policy knowledge graphs and intervention encodings
legacy_cells.AJ: GraphSAGE spatial encoder; relational graph neural network for policy knowledge graphs; Transformer encoder with cross-attention prediction head; all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence encoder for policy text embeddings
legacy_cells.AM: Policy strategies are retrieved in parallel from a shared vector-quantized codebook using state-context and policy-graph embeddings; projected strategy vectors are concatenated with spatial state embeddings, then processed temporally by a Transformer.
legacy_cells.BD: Policy identity/content encoded from legislative documents; policy enactment time is represented in the monthly historical sequence.
legacy_cells.BF: For optimization, search is restricted to a candidate policy pool of representative policies from five domains, augmented with state-specific enacted policy documents.
legacy_cells.BL: Monthly resolution; forecasting input window T_h = 6 months and forecast window T_f = 6 months.
legacy_cells.BN: Geographic state-adjacency graph for spatial aggregation; structured relational policy knowledge graph and vector-quantized canonical intervention-strategy codebook.
legacy_cells.BS: Predicted future state-level opioid overdose death trajectories.
legacy_cells.BT: Cross-attention prediction head projects historical-context representations to future opioid overdose outcomes at each forecast horizon.
legacy_cells.BU: Minimize cumulative predicted overdose deaths over the forecasting horizon.
legacy_cells.BV: Outcome prediction loss (squared error) plus lambda-weighted vector-quantization commitment loss.
legacy_cells.CI: D sequential decision periods; numeric planning horizon not specified.
legacy_cells.CK: Minimize cumulative predicted overdose deaths over the forecast horizon; candidate actions are policy choices from the defined policy pool.
legacy_cells.CV: No causal identification assumptions are established; the authors state that detailed confounding factors are not controlled and parallel-trends assumptions are not enforced.
legacy_cells.CX: Counterfactual trajectories are not directly validated against ground truth because outcomes are unobservable; credibility is based on factual forecasting accuracy.

limitations: Automated model review, not independent human verification or replication.
All 12 physical pages have supplied earlier API text/image review coverage. This synthesis read complete supplied text and attributed image-review notes, not image pixels directly.
Source hash, page-call receipts and local path were supplied, not recomputed or independently authenticated.
No repository, code, data download, trained weights, external cited full text or additional supplements were inspected or executed.
No executable schema, source-match, semantic or graph validation, filesystem save or KG admission was performed in this call.
Core membership is implemented history-based health-world prediction; full recursive socioeconomic-state propagation and latent successor transitions remain unresolved.
Dataset geography reports 48 states, whereas cross-state testing reports 40 training and 9 unseen states. Introductory feature-count wording differs from C=12 total channels.
CDC WONDER versus provisional-data source identity, mortality aggregation, normalization, release lag, missingness and monthly harmonization are unresolved.
Exact temporal split boundaries, sliding-window separation, train-only preprocessing and held-out-state graph/KG/codebook exposure are insufficiently documented.
Masked/next-token training claims are unreconciled with the detailed parallel prediction head and outcome-plus-VQ objective.
Tensor dimensions, central-node self-feature handling, codebook size, temperature, commitment weight, extraction prompts and extraction fidelity are incompletely reported.
Table 2 ± type and error aggregation/normalization are unspecified; descriptive mean rankings do not establish statistical significance.
Six months is maximum evaluated block extent, not an accepted effective horizon, recursive drift test or calibrated trajectory guarantee.
TN H 215 dates/identity conflict; later-dated policies are used in earlier hypothetical windows. Case-specific holdout status and pre-window policy advancement are unresolved.
MCTS searches and scores with the same predictor. No independent policy value, exploitation stress test, legal/cost feasibility or policy-pair synergy test is established.
R2 refers only to stated held-out actual retrospective aggregate human-outcome forecasting. R1 refers separately to in-silico technical search. R3 is partial, and R4–R8 are not established.
Raw legacy cells are preserved unchanged as historical extraction, including stale locators, missing fields and unsupported closed-loop implications.
